query: TC4 (Ti6Al4V) is an unmodified α + β dual-phase alloy whose low hardness and poor friction and wear properties limit its use under extreme-service and high-contact-stress conditions. Formulate one hypothesis for an intervention that could improve its hardness and wear resistance without sacrificing its existing beneficial properties. State the intervention, proposed mechanism, predicted outcome relative to untreated TC4, applicable operating or test boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment with an explicit result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Laser cladding a TiAl-based composite coating onto TC4 (Ti6Al4V) will significantly improve its surface hardness and wear resistance through the formation of hard, intermetallic phases and solid-solution strengthening, while retaining the substrate’s beneficial properties such as high strength-to-weight ratio and corrosion resistance.
generation.material_initial_state: TC4 (Ti6Al4V) in its unmodified α+β dual-phase condition with low hardness and poor friction and wear properties.
generation.intervention: Apply a TiAl-based composite coating via laser cladding, potentially incorporating minor Ni additions to promote the formation of intermetallic compounds.
generation.conditions: Tests conducted under room temperature sliding wear conditions with moderate to high contact stresses, typical of service environments encountered in aerospace and biomedical applications.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a reinforced surface layer consisting of hard intermetallic compounds (e.g., Fe2Ti, Ni3Ti, and Co2Ti) and a refined microstructure that enhances dislocation barrier effects.
generation.mechanism: Laser cladding promotes rapid solidification that leads to in-situ formation of intermetallic phases and solid solution strengthening; these modifications increase surface hardness and improve wear resistance while maintaining good metallurgical bonding with the substrate.
generation.predicted_outcome: The coated TC4 will exhibit a substantial increase (approximately 1.5–2 times) in surface hardness and a significant reduction in wear rate compared to untreated TC4, without adversely affecting its inherent light weight and corrosion resistance.
generation.baseline: Untreated TC4, which has relatively low microhardness and high wear rate under similar testing conditions.
generation.boundary: The improvement is expected under standard ambient conditions during sliding wear tests; however, the long-term adhesion of the coating and performance under extreme cyclic loading or high-temperature conditions remain to be further evaluated.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative improvements in hardness and wear rates, as well as the durability of the coating under prolonged service conditions, require further experimental validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set of untreated TC4 and another set of TC4 coated with the TiAl-based composite via laser cladding. Subject both sets to identical ball-on-disk sliding wear tests under controlled ambient conditions and identical loads. Characterize the surface hardness using Vickers microhardness testing and assess wear rates using mass loss and wear track profilometry. Additionally, perform microstructural analysis (e.g., SEM, XRD) to verify the formation of the intended intermetallic phases.
measurements: Coefficient of friction during sliding tests
Phase identification and microstructure characterization via SEM/XRD
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the TC4 samples with the laser-clad TiAl-based coating do not show at least a 20% increase in hardness and a 15% reduction in wear rate compared to the untreated samples, or if the microstructural analysis does not confirm the formation of the intended intermetallic phases, then the hypothesis is falsified.

In this study, TiAl metal-based coatings were prepared through laser cladding to improve the wear resistance of TC4 via solid solution strengthening []. The phase compositions and microstructural phases of (TiAl)95−xCu5Nix (where x = 0, 3, 6, and 9 at.%) coatings with varying Ni content were investigated through various characterization methods and performance tests. The coatings were evaluated for hardness, wear resistance, and mechanical properties, and their microstructures were analyzed to extensively elucidate the mechanism underlying the changes in coating properties. The study concluded with an in-depth exploration of TiAl alloys, revealing the relationship between their microstructure and properties. This research offers a theoretical foundation and technical guidance for optimizing the preparation process and improving the properties of TiAl alloys. Additionally, the findings offer new insights and directions for applying TiAl alloys in aerospace, automotive, and biomedical fields.

High hardness and good wear resistance have been revealed for the high-entropy alloy (HEA) system AlCoCrFeNiTi, confirming the potential for surface protection applications. Detailed studies to investigate the microstructure and phase formation have been carried out using different production routes. Powder metallurgical technologies allow for much higher flexibility in the customisation of materials compared to casting processes. Particularly, spark plasma sintering (SPS) enables the fast processing of the feedstock, the suppression of grain coarsening and the production of samples with a low porosity. Furthermore, solid lubricants can be incorporated for the improvement of wear resistance and the reduction of the coefficient of friction (COF). This study focuses on the production of AlCoCrFeNiTi composites comprising solid lubricants. Bulk materials with a MoS2 content of up to 15 wt % were produced. The wear resistance and COF were investigated in detail under sliding wear conditions in ball-on-disk tests at room temperature and elevated temperature.
